source: Fleming et al. (2010) Relating introspective accuracy to individual differences in brain structure (Science)
finding: 32 people did a visual 2-choice task kept near 71% correct, then rated confidence 1-6. Skill at linking confidence to accuracy (Aroc) varied widely between people even though task accuracy did not. It tracked gray matter in right anterior prefrontal cortex (BA10).
numbers: N=32. Aroc range 0.55-0.75 while accuracy 70-74%. Aroc vs accuracy r=-0.11 (P=0.56). Split-half reliability of Aroc r=0.69. BA10 peak t=4.8, P<0.05 whole-brain corrected.
quote: metacognitive ability ... correlated with gray matter volume in right anterior prefrontal cortex
limits: One lab, small sample, visual task only. Left BA10 did not survive correction. Single-sample structural correlation, the kind that often shrinks on replication.
agent_relevance: Reading one's own certainty is a separate skill from being right: two agents with equal accuracy can differ in how well confidence tracks correctness. Measure it separately, never assume it follows accuracy.

source: Fleming et al. (2010) Relating introspective accuracy to individual differences in brain structure (Science)
finding: Control analyses: the brain-structure link was specific to metacognitive sensitivity, not to task performance or to how confident people were overall.
numbers: BA10 volume vs d' r=0.15 P=0.42; vs Broc (bias to use high confidence) r=-0.023 P=0.90. Negative correlation in left inferior temporal gyrus, tmax=4.66.
limits: Dissociation rests on non-significant correlations in N=32.
agent_relevance: Bias (how high confidence runs) and sensitivity (does confidence separate right from wrong) are different quantities. A scaffold should check discrimination, not mean confidence.

source: Mazancieux et al. (2020) Is there a G factor for metacognition?
finding: Large sample (N=181) tested whether confidence skill is one general ability. Average confidence level correlated across four tasks. Metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d') also correlated across tasks in a hierarchical Bayesian model, even where first-order accuracy did not.
numbers: N=181, four 2AFC tasks (episodic memory, semantic memory, executive function, visual perception). 5 of 6 cross-task correlations in meta-d'/d' significant. Accuracy correlations across tasks ranged r=-0.08 to r=0.25. Efficiency higher for the two memory tasks than for executive or visual tasks.
quote: at least some components of metacognitive efficiency in retrospective confidence are domain general
limits: Earlier work often found null cross-domain links, attributed here to low power. French-speaking sample, 2AFC only. Only 'some components' are general.
agent_relevance: Partly general confidence skill supports using one confidence read-out across task types, but expect per-domain differences in how good it is. Calibrate per task family.

source: Rahnev & Fleming (2019) How experimental procedures influence estimates of metacognitive ability
finding: Re-analysis of earlier data: staircase procedures that vary stimulus difficulty inflate every common measure of metacognitive ability, because easy and hard trials differ in accuracy and people can tell them apart. So part of 'good confidence' is just knowing which items are easy.
numbers: N=31. All-contrast vs 1-contrast: type-2 AUC +0.034, t(30)=3.18, P=0.003, Cohen's d=0.57; meta-d'-d' diff 0.253, d=0.63. 3-contrast vs all-contrast d>0.66 for all measures. First-order d' did not differ across conditions (F(2,60)=0.71, P=0.49).
limits: Reanalysis of one published dataset. Bang et al. 2019 reported a similar effect for meta-d'/d'.
agent_relevance: Item-difficulty variance makes confidence look informative. A confidence signal that mostly reflects 'this item type is easy' is weaker evidence than it looks; test within matched difficulty.

source: Rahnev et al. (2022) Consensus goals in the field of visual metacognition
finding: 26 researchers set goals for visual metacognition. They state that few confidence findings have been independently replicated and that effect sizes for factors affecting confidence are rarely compared.
numbers: Consensus of 26 researchers; four long-term and two medium-term goals.
quote: few of the studies cited above have been independently replicated
limits: Position paper, no new data. Visual-perception focus.
agent_relevance: Human confidence research has a thin replication base. Treat specific effect sizes with care when borrowing them as design rules.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when options are shown in lettered format. Calibration improves with size and few-shot prompting. Replacing an option with 'none of the above' hurts accuracy and calibration.
numbers: Models up to 52B. Calibration improves from zero-shot to few-shot (Figure 4).
limits: Base models, 2022. Format dependent. Not the same as open-ended generation.
agent_relevance: Confidence is only usable when the question is framed as a choice among visible options; asking in free form changes it.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: RLHF policies look badly miscalibrated, but one temperature change (T=2.5) largely repairs it on several tasks. RL fine-tuning sharpens outputs rather than destroying the information.
numbers: Same T=2.5 for all evaluations; MMLU, MMLU true/false, TruthfulQA, 52B.
quote: a simple temperature adjustment ... largely fixes calibration issues
limits: Authors note heavier RL may distort calibration beyond what temperature can fix.
agent_relevance: Tuned chat models need re-calibration, not blind trust. A post-hoc map from raw score to hit rate is cheap.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Self-evaluation P(True): the model proposes an answer then rates if it is true. Zero-shot it sits near 50% and is poorly calibrated. Showing the model 5 of its own samples at T=1 before judging one improves it a lot. Larger k mostly improves calibration, not AUROC.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval, arithmetic. 5 samples shown at T=1. Figure 1: filtering to P(True)>0.5 raises accuracy on every task.
limits: Models find own samples more plausible, so the task is harder than judging human-written options. Exact AUROC values are in figures, not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Support for comparing an answer against several independent samples (consistency) rather than asking the model once if it is right.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK), a trained 'do I know this' probability read before any answer, is predicted well in-distribution, rises appropriately with source material and with hints, but is poorly calibrated on new task types.
numbers: Trained on final-token P(IK); tests include source passages (trivia) and GSM8k hints. Models are only somewhat better at their own P(IK) than at another model's.
limits: Requires labelled training; calibration breaks out of distribution (Figure 13).
agent_relevance: A learned 'can I solve this' gate may help routing, but it must be re-checked on each new task family.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Asked to state confidence in words, black-box LLMs are overconfident (imitating human talk). GPT-4 gets lower ECE but verbalized confidence barely separates right from wrong (AUROC about 62.7%).
numbers: 8 tasks, 5 models (GPT-3, Vicuna, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 Chat). Vanilla verbalized ECE averaged above 0.377 for weaker models. GPT-4 mean AUROC 62.7% vs 50% chance.
quote: verbalized confidence ... tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns
limits: Black-box elicitation only; dataset coverage includes professional-knowledge tasks, where all methods struggle.
agent_relevance: Core support for SCHEMA 4b: do not use stated certainty to stop; it is overconfident and weakly discriminating.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Prompting tricks lower calibration error without improving discrimination. With CoT on GSM8K, GPT-4 (93.6% accurate) gets ECE 0.064 just by saying 100% every time.
numbers: Confidence stays in the 80-100% band; failure-prediction AUROC stays near 0.5.
limits: A low ECE can come from a constant answer. Trap for anyone judging by ECE alone.
agent_relevance: Judge confidence signals by discrimination (AUROC, or accuracy gain after filtering), not ECE.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Agreement across several sampled answers predicts errors far better than the model's own stated number.
numbers: 5 samples with consistency aggregation: GSM8K AUROC rose from 54.8% (verbalized, near chance) to 92.7%. Gains saturate as samples grow from M=1 to M=13.
quote: consistency among multiple responses is more effective ... compared to verbalized confidence
limits: Gain is largest on arithmetic with a single checkable answer. Costs M times the compute.
agent_relevance: Direct support for sample consistency as the stop/escalate signal, with a small M (about 5) giving most of the gain.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: White-box token probabilities do only a little better than black-box methods; none of the methods wins everywhere and all weaken on hard professional-knowledge tasks.
numbers: AUROC gap between white-box and best black-box 0.522 to 0.605 in the abstract. Best aggregation lowers ECE to 0.028; Avg-Conf best for failure prediction.
limits: Aggregation choice matters by dataset; no universal winner.
agent_relevance: Do not tune the confidence method on one benchmark and expect it to carry over.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Model size helps but not enough: moving GPT-3 to GPT-4 raised AUROC by about 22%, and ECE fell, yet failure prediction stays far from ideal.
numbers: Reported as approximately 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4 (Table 2).
limits: Table values varied by task.
agent_relevance: Waiting for a bigger model will not solve this; the check must be built into the loop.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, the verbalized number is better calibrated than the token probability. Asking for several candidate answers first (considering the opposite) cuts calibration error further.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, TriviaQA: ECE label prob 0.140 vs verbalized one-stage top-4 0.054; AUC 0.869 vs 0.896. SciQ ECE 0.256 vs 0.065. ECE cut by a relative 50% or more on many cells.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Calibration gain is partly from less extreme numbers; AUC changes are small on TriviaQA. Tested on ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2 (mid-2023).
agent_relevance: Tension with Xiong: verbalized numbers can give lower ECE yet little discrimination. Use ECE-style gains only as a post-hoc rescaling, not as a decision signal.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: On TruthfulQA, token probabilities have AUC below 0.5, so confidence ranks wrong answers above right ones when the model repeats common misconceptions.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo: TruthfulQA label prob ECE 0.451, AUC 0.418; 'Is True' prob AUC 0.384; entropy AUC 0.236.
limits: Specific to adversarial misconception questions.
agent_relevance: Where a popular wrong answer exists, high agreement can mean a shared misconception. Consistency fails on adversarially popular errors.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough. Fine-tuning on about 1,000 graded examples (LoRA plus prompt) beats sampling and verbalized baselines on both ECE and AUROC. Sampling methods calibrate fine but discriminate weakly; verbal elicitation discriminates moderately but calibrates poorly.
numbers: MMLU multiple-choice and open-ended; sampling baseline K=10. Zero-shot ECE does not improve with a better base model; AUROC improves only slightly.
limits: Needs labels and weights access. Sampling baseline costs O(K^2) clustering.
agent_relevance: Cheap supervised calibrator is strongest when weights are open; for a prompt-only agent it points back to consistency plus held-out checking.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Uncertainty estimators transfer across models: Mistral 7B applied to LLaMA-2 7B had better AUROC than LLaMA-2 7B on itself. A model trained on incorrect answers still did well, so part of the skill is learning which questions are hard.
numbers: Probe, sBERT and OpenAI-embedding variants were competitive. Ablation with incorrect answers close to Probe but worse than sampled-answer training.
limits: Part of the signal is a question-difficulty shortcut. Training sets were small.
agent_relevance: Another model (or a second pass) can judge reliability of a first answer; self-access to internals is not required.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Users tracked calibrated confidence scores when deciding to accept model answers, and ignored a random confidence baseline.
numbers: N=181 crowdworkers, about 20 per variant, multiple-choice exam with Mistral 7B Instruct; reliance varied most with LoRA+Probe scores.
limits: Preliminary study, crowd sample.
agent_relevance: Shown confidence changes human reliance only if it is informative; a useless display costs trust.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by meaning and takes entropy over meaning clusters. It predicts correctness better than length-normalised token entropy, lexical similarity and p(True), with the gap growing with model size and sample count.
numbers: 10 samples per question. AUROC 0.83 (TriviaQA) and 0.77 (CoQA) vs counting distinct answers 0.79 and 0.66. Mean distinct meanings: 3.89 for wrong vs 1.89 for right (TriviaQA); 1.77 vs 1.27 (CoQA).
quote: semantic entropy has a significantly higher AUROC than entropy in sequence-probability-space
limits: Needs an entailment model for clustering; greedy decoding gives no signal. Short factual answers; open-ended long text is harder.
agent_relevance: Count distinct meanings across samples, not distinct strings. Wrong answers show about twice the variety.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Reasoning models that think long express better calibrated confidence than non-reasoning versions, in 33 of 36 settings, even where they are less accurate.
numbers: 6 reasoning models, 6 datasets. GLM-Z1 had 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4 on NonambigQA yet 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Calibration improves as the chain of thought unfolds.
limits: Non-reasoning models can win on AUROC on multiple-choice sets because option cues give a free hint (95% vs 85% bins).
agent_relevance: Longer, self-checking thinking makes verbalized confidence more informative, but the option-cue artifact warns against reading AUROC from two bins.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Ablation: removing slow thinking (backtracking, alternatives) from the trace hurts calibration most; explicit reasoning about confidence matters little. Non-reasoning models improve when guided to slow-think in context.
numbers: TriviaQA ECE: original 0.042; without non-linear reasoning 0.161; no CoT 0.150. NonambigQA AUROC 0.749 original, 0.728 without non-linear reasoning, 0.618 no CoT. Removing epistemic phrases: ECE worse but AUROC up to 0.837 on NonambigQA.
limits: One model family per ablation.
agent_relevance: Calibration comes from actually re-solving or exploring alternatives, not from the model musing on its own certainty.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Humans reading default LLM explanations overestimate how often the LLM is right and cannot tell right from wrong. Longer explanations raise confidence without adding accuracy.
numbers: N=301 across experiments (about 40 each in Exp 1, 60 in Exp 2). Human AUC 0.589 and 0.602 (MC, GPT-3.5, PaLM2) and 0.592 (GPT-4o short answer); model AUC 0.751, 0.746, 0.781. Long vs short explanations BF=25; mean AUC 0.54 for long, 0.57 uncertainty-only.
quote: longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy
limits: Older models and trivia-style questions. Participants had no direct access to numeric confidence.
agent_relevance: Verbose reasoning looks more reliable than it is. G10 holds: reasoning text is not evidence; do not let length raise trust.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Rewriting explanations to match the model's real confidence narrowed both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap for people.
numbers: Wording changes ('I am not sure' vs 'somewhat sure' vs high) shifted human confidence, BF>100 in Exp 2a, 2b, 2c.
limits: One prompt style; effect on actual task accuracy not shown.
agent_relevance: Hedging words move human confidence strongly, so they must carry a real signal or be omitted.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned to write 'X% confidence' after its answer was calibrated, stayed moderately calibrated under a shift from add/subtract to multiply/divide and multi-answer questions, and beat a constant baseline.
numbers: CalibratedMath suite; MSE and MAD metrics. Verbalized and logit-based both generalize; trained only on add-subtract.
limits: Fine-tuned, arithmetic domain. Summary table text was garbled in extraction, so exact cell values are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Learned verbal confidence can transfer, but only after supervised training; zero-shot it does not.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Share of sampled reasoning paths that agree with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K, so low consistency flags low confidence.
numbers: Figure 5: GSM8K agreement vs accuracy. Imperfect CoT prompts: greedy 17.1 -> 14.9; self-consistency with 40 paths: 23.4 (LaMDA-137B).
quote: self-consistency confers some ability for the model to 'know when it doesn't know'
limits: Reported as a figure, no AUROC. Shared systematic errors give high consistency with a wrong answer.
agent_relevance: Earliest evidence for using vote share as the certainty signal in a scaffold.

source: Geng et al. (2024) A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in LLMs
finding: Survey separates logit-based, consistency-based, verbalized and trained confidence methods. Notes that outputs have exponentially many forms and many wordings share one meaning, so confidence must work on meaning.
numbers: Abstract and start only were read; no figures taken.
limits: Not read in full; do not cite its numbers.
agent_relevance: Use as a map to find further LLM calibration papers.
